title: Ombudsman decision DRN-6398019 — AXA Insurance UK Plc
text:
DRN-6398019

The complaint

Mr H and Ms L complain that AXA has declined to cover an escape of water claim made
under their home insurance policy.

Mr H and Ms L are joint policyholders. As Mr H dealt with the claim and referred the
complaint to our Service, I mainly refer to him in this decision.

References to AXA include its agents.

What happened
In brief summary, Mr H holds buildings insurance with AXA for his home. The property
shares a party wall with a neighbouring gatehouse. The ground floor of the gatehouse
includes an archway and driveway, with the rest of the building above it. Part of Mr H’s
property sits below the level of the gatehouse driveway.

In 2023, Mr H discovered damp and water damage to the inside of the party wall, including
damage to the plaster and carpet.

Several years earlier, works had taken place at the neighbouring property that had damaged
the party wall. Those issues were dealt with. But because of the location of the damp, Mr H
arranged for the party wall surveyor involved in that matter to inspect the property again. The
surveyor concluded the dampness was longstanding and linked both to previous damp-
proofing measures and to a leaking rainwater downpipe belonging to the gatehouse.

AXA also arranged an inspection through its loss adjusters. The adjusters identified the
leaking rainwater pipe but couldn’t confirm the exact cause of the damage.
AXA declined the claim. It said the damage had resulted from faulty damp-proofing which
wasn’t covered by the policy. Mr H provided further comments from the surveyor, who said
the leaking pipe was the only obvious source of moisture in the area and recommended Mr
H contact the neighbour urgently to arrange a repair.

AXA maintained its position. It said there hadn’t been a sudden, unforeseen escape of water
from within Mr H’s property, and the issue was instead caused by longstanding drainage
issues outside the property.

Mr H didn’t think this was fair so referred the matter to our Service.

The complaint came to me. I issued a provisional decision setting out why I intended to
uphold the complaint, and to direct AXA to accept the claim and pay compensation. I said:
“Where there’s a dispute about what’s happened, I’ve based my decision on the balance of
probabilities – in other words, on what I consider is most likely to have happened in the light
of the available evidence.

Mr H’s policy covers damage caused by “water escaping from fixed, domestic: pipes, boilers,
water tanks, toilets”. The policy also excludes damage caused by faulty workmanship or
design, and damage caused gradually.

AXA says there hasn’t been an insured escape of water and the damage was instead
caused by faulty damp-proofing and long-standing drainage issues. So, I’ve considered
whether there was an escape of water, whether that most likely caused the damage, and
whether AXA has shown a policy exclusion applies.

I’m satisfied there’s been an escape of water from the neighbouring pipe. There doesn’t
appear to be any real dispute that this has been leaking. The surveyor found “significant past
water leakage” from the pipe along with signs of ongoing water ingress. AXA’s loss adjuster
accepted the pipe was leaking and said the internal damage was consistent with the route of
the pipe. He also noted there was no evidence of any other ongoing leaks.

I’ve considered AXA’s position that the leak originated from outside the property. But the
policy wording doesn’t say the pipe has to be within the property, nor does it limit cover only
to internal pipework. I’ve also seen internal correspondence where AXA confirmed the policy
doesn’t exclude pipes in a neighbouring property and acknowledged that it “would be hard
pushed to decline the claim” on that basis. While those comments don’t decide the matter,
they do support my view that the policy doesn’t rule out neighbouring leaks.

I’ve considered AXA’s position that the damage is due to faulty damp-proofing. AXA has
mainly relied on the findings of the party wall surveyor to reach that conclusion, so I’ve
considered those findings carefully.

The surveyor’s initial report suggested the dampness was longstanding and the existing
damp-proof membrane, installed at some point in the past, may have created a “damming
effect” as it wasn’t high enough compared to the neighbouring driveway. But the surveyor
also concluded the rainwater pipe had exacerbated the problem. He said:

“Based on our findings, we believe the dampness in the lower ground floor is a long-
standing issue where previous remedial measures, including the installation of a
damp-proof membrane, have created a damming effect. Due to the membrane not
extending to the appropriate level, moisture has come through above this. This issue
has likely been exacerbated by prolonged rainwater leakage from the gatehouse.”

I don’t think the surveyor’s conclusions are enough for AXA to fairly say the damage had
been caused by the faulty damp-proofing, and not by the leaking pipe.

I say that because the surveyor later explained that if the damp-proofing had failed because
of the works several years before, he would’ve expected the damp to have arisen much
earlier. Mr H has said he’s lived at the property for more than 20 years and the issue has
only arisen now. The surveyor also said that the pipe was the only obvious source of
moisture in the area and recommended urgent repairs to it.

With all that in mind, I think the evidence points more strongly towards the leaking pipe as
the main cause of the damage. I accept it may have exposed an issue with the damp
proofing, but I don’t think Mr H would reasonably have known about that given the leak has
arisen from within the structure of the wall.
The pipe is also partly within the wall structure and is not Mr H’s to maintain. So, I don’t think
it was fair for AXA to conclude that the leaking pipe wasn’t the main cause of the damage.

I’m also not persuaded the policy exclusion for faulty workmanship or design can fairly apply
here. For an insurer to rely on an exclusion like that, we’d expect them to show exactly how
the property was defective relative to the standards in place at the time. I haven’t seen
evidence to show when the damp-proofing was installed or whether it failed to meet the
building standards at that time.

AXA has also said the damage wasn’t caused by a sudden one-off event. I acknowledge the
point, but the policy doesn’t require an escape of water to be sudden or one-off. I accept the
evidence suggests the leak may have developed over time. But, as I’ve said above, I haven’t
seen evidence that Mr H knew or ought reasonably to have known the damage was
occurring before it became visible, or that he could reasonably prevent it.

In conclusion, I don’t think AXA has shown it was fair to decline the claim. In the
circumstances, I’m satisfied on balance that the main cause of the damage was most likely
the water escaping from the neighbouring pipe, and I’m not persuaded AXA has shown that
isn’t covered.

Putting things right

To resolve the complaint, I intend to require AXA to accept the claim. That means it will have
to consider the claim against the remaining policy terms and assess whether any costs Mr H
has reasonably incurred should be reimbursed to him.

Mr H has said he’s incurred costs investigating the leak and taking legal action against the
neighbour. I think it’s fair that AXA has a chance to consider those costs and how best to
progress the claim. Mr H should provide evidence of his costs to AXA for its consideration. If
Mr H is unhappy with how AXA settles the claim, he can raise a further complaint about that,
and refer it to our Service if he remains unhappy.

Mr H has mentioned higher premiums from having a declined claim on his record. AXA will
need to amend any relevant internal and external databases to reflect the accurate claim
position. With the claim accepted, I don't think Mr H will be any worse off in relation to his
premiums than he would have been with it declined. Accepting the claim earlier would likely
have meant he paid at least as much in premiums as he did with a declined claim.

However, I do think AXA declining the claim has caused Mr H unnecessary distress and
inconvenience. He’s had to spend a lot of time and effort obtaining evidence and pursuing
the matter after AXA maintained its decline of the claim. So, I intend to award Mr H £300
compensation to reflect that impact.”

Responses

Mr H broadly accepted my provisional findings. But he questioned whether AXA acted in
good faith given its internal correspondence about not declining the claim. Mr H also asked
that I increase my compensation award to reflect the time and effort he’s spent pursuing the
matter, including dealing with his neighbour and starting court action.

AXA didn’t accept my provisional findings. It said Mr H’s policy wording only covers escapes
of water from “fixed, internal pipes” and so a leaking rainwater pipe shouldn’t be covered.
AXA also maintained that certain exclusions should apply, such as damage caused
gradually, by wear and tear, by a failure to fix a known issue, or by damp.

AXA asked that if I maintain my provisional findings that I limit any settlement amount to the
damage in Mr H’s home and the policy limits under Mr H’s trace and access cover.

As both parties have responded, I now consider it appropriate to issue my final decision.

What I’ve decided – and why
I’ve considered all the available evidence and arguments to decide what’s fair and reasonable

in the circumstances of this complaint.
For the reasons I set out in my provisional decision, and having considered the further
comments from both parties, I haven’t found reason to reach a different outcome. So, I
uphold this complaint.

I acknowledge Mr H’s point about AXA’s internal correspondence. However, it isn’t my role
to determine AXA’s motives or whether it acted in bad faith. My role is to decide whether
AXA treated Mr H fairly and reasonably. And, for the reasons I’ve given, I’m satisfied it didn’t.

I’ve considered Mr H’s request for more compensation. I appreciate he’s spent lots of time
and effort pursuing the matter, gathering evidence, and dealing with his dispute with his
neighbour. However, the complaint I’ve had to decide is about AXA’s decision to decline the
claim. I’m not deciding the value of the claim itself or whether certain costs connected to the
dispute with the neighbour should ultimately be paid under the policy, or whether those costs
and steps would ultimately have been necessary anyway.

Taking everything into account, including Mr H’s further comments, I remain of the view that
£300 fairly reflects the distress and inconvenient caused by AXA’s decline.

I’ve also considered AXA’s response regarding the correct policy wording. AXA says the
policy only covers escapes of water from “fixed, internal pipes”. That isn’t the wording I relied
on in my provisional decision. The wording I relied on referred to “fixed, domestic pipes”.
That wording is included in the policy booklet Mr H provided; it matches the policy booklet
available on AXA’s website for the relevant period; it was quoted in reports from AXA’s loss
adjuster; and it was quoted in the decline letter AXA sent to Mr H. So, on balance, I’m
satisfied I’ve relied on the right wording, and the policy does not limit cover to internal pipes.

I’ve carefully considered the exclusions AXA has referred to. However, I remain of the view
that it isn’t fair to apply them here.

I haven’t seen evidence that Mr H knew or ought reasonably to have known about the leak
before the damage was visible in his home. I also don’t think it would be fair to treat the
damage as having been caused by damp rather than by an escape of water, given the
expert commentary about the source of the water. I also don’t think it would be fair to apply
exclusions for damage caused by wear and tear or a failure to fix a known issue. I say that
because I don’t think it would be fair to impose a requirement on Mr H to maintain a part of
the building for which I haven’t seen he’s responsible, or that he ought reasonably to have
known that damage like this was likely to occur.

Finally, I’ve considered AXA’s comments about the scope of any potential settlement. It isn’t
appropriate for me to make findings about exactly how the claim should be valued or settled.
The complaint referred to our Service was that AXA unfairly declined the claim. My decision
is that AXA shouldn’t have done that. It follows that AXA must now deal with the claim in
accordance with the remaining terms and conditions of the policy.
For the avoidance of doubt, any questions about the extent of cover, the value of the claim,
trace and access costs, third-party repairs, or any other aspect of the settlement, are matters
for AXA to consider in the first instance.

If Mr H finds that he’s unhappy with the way AXA goes on to settle the claim, he’ll be entitled
to raise a further complaint about that. But, it doesn’t form part of the complaint I’m deciding
here.

To conclude, I’ve considered the matter again and my opinion hasn’t changed. Therefore,
my provisional decision along with my additional comments here now form the basis of this,
my final decision.

Putting things right
To resolve the complaint, I direct AXA to:

•
accept the claim.

•
pay Mr H and Ms L £300 of compensation for distress and inconvenience.

My final decision
For the reasons I’ve given, I uphold Mr H and Ms L’s complaint and direct AXA Insurance UK
Plc to do as I’ve set out above.

Under the rules of the Financial Ombudsman Service, I’m required to ask Mr H and Ms L to
accept or reject my decision before 30 June 2026.

Chris Woolaway
Ombudsman
